name: Bangladesh
governanceModel: Draft risk-based national AI policy atop a newly enacted data-protection law, carried across a 2026 change of government
debateTopics: Whether an ambitious draft AI policy can survive Bangladesh's institutional-capacity and political-transition gap
Data-protection and cyber laws that critics argue protect the state more than citizens
A vast freelancer and BPO workforce exposed to AI automation, with thin domestic Bengali-model capacity
Reliance on a single national data centre and new data-localisation rules for 'sovereign' AI
overview:
Bangladesh's AI-governance story is inseparable from an unusually turbulent political period. The long-serving Awami League government of Sheikh Hasina fell in early August 2024 amid a student-led uprising, and an interim government headed by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus took charge on 8 August 2024. That interim administration governed by ordinance until a general election on 12 February 2026, which the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won; Tarique Rahman was sworn in as Prime Minister on 17 February 2026. Much of the country's most consequential digital and AI-related lawmaking therefore straddles a change of government, and it is important to be careful about which administration produced which instrument — the interim government drafted and gazetted several measures that the elected BNP government has since inherited, amended or is still finalising.

On AI specifically, Bangladesh has a lineage of ambition that has repeatedly outrun implementation. A draft National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence circulated under the previous government around 2019-2020, and the ICT Division published a draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy in 2024; commentators note that little of the earlier roadmap materialised. The interim government advanced a more detailed National AI Policy 2026-2030, whose Draft v2.0 was released for public consultation that closed on 8 February 2026 — a risk-based, four-tier framework that would prohibit real-time public biometric surveillance, social scoring and AI-enabled weapons, mandate algorithmic impact assessments for high-risk systems, create a coordinating National Data Governance and Innovation Agency (NDGIA), and signal an intention to join the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on AI. As of mid-2026 the policy remains a draft, and the incoming BNP government has said it is finalising a broadly similar 'human-centric' national AI policy, so continuity across the transition appears likely but is not yet settled. The proposed NDGIA does not yet exist operationally.

Underpinning this is a digital-government apparatus centred on the ICT Division (within the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology) and its flagship a2i (Aspire to Innovate) programme, historically UNDP-supported and now reportedly being restructured into a more autonomous statutory agency. Bangladesh's economic AI narrative leans heavily on a very large online-freelancer and business-process-outsourcing (BPO) workforce — frequently described as among the world's largest sources of online freelancers — and on 'Digital Bangladesh' and 'Smart Bangladesh 2041' branding, though the latter was a Hasina-era slogan whose status under successive governments should be read cautiously. Compute remains nascent and import-reliant, anchored by a single state-owned Tier-IV national data centre at Kaliakoir; there is no frontier-model developer and only a handful of firms building Bengali-language models. On adjacent law, the interim government gazetted a Personal Data Protection Ordinance in November 2025 (later amended and then passed into a Personal Data Protection Act, 2026) and replaced the controversial Cyber Security Act 2023 with a Cyber Security Ordinance 2025 — reforms welcomed in part but criticised for continuing to shield the state.

currentDirection.summary: Bangladesh appears to be moving from having essentially no dedicated AI or data-governance framework toward one: a first comprehensive data-protection law is now in force, a reformed cyber ordinance has replaced the 2023 Act, and a risk-based national AI policy sits in advanced draft. The direction is therefore toward more formal regulation, but implementation is genuinely uncertain — the coordinating AI agency the policy envisages does not yet exist, the AI policy is unadopted, and the whole agenda has just passed from an interim government to a newly elected one whose priorities are still being set out.

recentDevelopments.text: The incoming BNP government's Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology, under minister Fakir Mahbub Anam Swapan, says Bangladesh is finalising a 'human-centric' National AI Policy focused on ethical, safe and inclusive AI use — broadly continuing the risk-based draft inherited from the interim government.

Bangladesh reportedly puts forward four priorities for global AI governance (inclusion, capacity-building, affordable connectivity and digital public goods) at international fora, positioning itself as a Global South voice rather than a model-building power.

The Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 comes into force (reported around 15 April 2026), replacing the 2025 Ordinance to become Bangladesh's first comprehensive data-protection law; commentators welcome the framework but criticise broad state and law-enforcement exemptions and executive-appointed oversight.

Following the 12 February 2026 general election won by the BNP, the interim government of Muhammad Yunus hands over to an elected government; Tarique Rahman is sworn in as Prime Minister on 17 February 2026, and Fakir Mahbub Anam Swapan takes over the Posts, Telecommunications and IT portfolio — reshaping the political ownership of Bangladesh's AI and digital agenda.

The interim government's ICT Division — whose posts/telecoms/ICT brief was led by Special Assistant Faiz Ahmad Taiyeb — releases the National AI Policy 2026-2030 Draft v2.0 for public review (consultation closing 8 February 2026): a four-tier risk-based framework prohibiting real-time public biometric surveillance, social scoring and AI-enabled weapons, requiring algorithmic impact assessments, and proposing a coordinating National Data Governance and Innovation Agency.

The President promulgates the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026 (Ordinance No. 23 of 2026), amending the 2025 Ordinance to tighten data-localisation/residency requirements — including keeping a synchronised in-country copy of restricted data and data held by critical information infrastructure.

The interim government gazettes the Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025, Bangladesh's first comprehensive personal-data instrument, establishing consent-based data rights while drawing early criticism over exemptions favouring the state.

Bangladesh's IT/BPO outsourcing exports are reported to be approaching US$1bn, buoyed by an AI-services push and one of the world's largest online-freelancer workforces — a central plank of the country's economic AI narrative even as domestic model-building stays thin.

policyAndRegulation.title: National AI Policy 2026-2030 (Draft)
policyAndRegulation.summary: A risk-based framework advanced by the ICT Division under the interim government (Draft v2.0 released February 2026, public consultation closed 8 February 2026) and reportedly being finalised in similar 'human-centric' form by the elected BNP government. It proposes four risk tiers (prohibited, high-risk, and lower categories), bans on real-time public biometric surveillance, social scoring and AI-enabled weapons, mandatory algorithmic impact assessments for high-risk systems, a coordinating National Data Governance and Innovation Agency (NDGIA), and possible accession to the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI. As of mid-2026 it remains a draft and the NDGIA does not yet exist operationally.

policyAndRegulation.title: Personal Data Protection Act, 2026
policyAndRegulation.summary: Bangladesh's first comprehensive data-protection law. It began as the Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2025 (gazetted 6 November 2025 by the interim government), was amended by Ordinance No. 23 of 2026 (5 February 2026) to strengthen data-localisation requirements, and was reported to come into force as an Act around April 2026 under the new Parliament. It sets consent-based data rights and data-residency rules but has been widely criticised for broad exemptions for the state and law-enforcement and for executive control over oversight.

policyAndRegulation.title: Cyber Security Ordinance, 2025
policyAndRegulation.summary: Promulgated by the interim government in May 2025 (Ordinance No. 25 of 2025), repealing the controversial Cyber Security Act 2023 and striking down around nine speech-related provisions that had been used to prosecute critics. Reform groups welcomed the softer penalties and more bailable offences but warned that surveillance and content-control powers relevant to AI-generated content and platform governance persist.

policyAndRegulation.title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence / National AI Policy 2024 (Draft, superseded)
policyAndRegulation.summary: An earlier lineage of AI policymaking: a draft National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence circulated under the previous government around 2019-2020, followed by a draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy published by the ICT Division in 2024. Neither was formally adopted, and commentary notes that little of the earlier roadmap was implemented; both have effectively been overtaken by the 2026-2030 draft.

researchEcosystem.summary: Bangladesh's AI research is predominantly academic and NLP-focused. The BUET CSE NLP Group has produced widely used Bengali/multilingual resources (e.g. work on Bangla language models and the XL-Sum multilingual summarisation dataset), while the University of Dhaka and BRAC University run Bangla NLP and data-science research and American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB) hosts an AI & Machine Learning group. Commercial capacity is comparatively thin: analysts note that very few firms are training Bengali-specific large language models despite 170m-plus Bengali speakers, with early efforts including Hishab Technologies' 'titulm' models and Intelsense AI's 'Ekush'. The picture is one of strong low-resource-language research talent but limited domestic compute and commercialisation.

companies.name: Hishab Technologies
companies.description: Dhaka-based voice-AI and Bangla NLP company experimenting with homegrown bilingual large language models (its 'titulm' family) and Bangla writing tools ('Shuddhi', pitched as a 'Grammarly for Bangla'); among the few local firms building Bengali-specific models.

companies.name: Intelsense AI
companies.description: Bangladeshi startup that launched 'Ekush', promoted as a model trained specifically on Bangla, with proprietary voice-AI applied across telemedicine, agriculture and other sectors.

companies.name: Brain Station 23
companies.description: One of Bangladesh's largest software and IT-services firms (publicly listed), delivering outsourced engineering and increasingly AI/ML-enabled solutions to domestic and international clients.

companies.name: Pathao
companies.description: Dhaka-headquartered ride-hailing and 'super-app' platform (also operating in Nepal) that applies machine learning to logistics, pricing and fintech across a large Bangladeshi user base.

providers.name: BDCCL National Data Centre (G-Cloud)
providers.description: State-owned Tier-IV national data centre at Bangabandhu/Kaliakoir Hi-Tech Park operated by Bangladesh Data Center Company Ltd, hosting government 'G-Cloud' services, storage and colocation — the backbone of public-sector digital infrastructure.

providers.name: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
providers.description: Global hyperscaler widely used by Bangladeshi startups and enterprises, served from nearby regions (e.g. Singapore/Mumbai) rather than an in-country region.

providers.name: Microsoft Azure
providers.description: Cloud provider used across Bangladeshi enterprise and public-sector workloads, without a dedicated in-country region.

providers.name: Google Cloud
providers.description: Cloud provider used by Bangladeshi developers and enterprises, served from regional data centres outside the country.

computeFrontier.compute: Nascent and import-reliant; centred on the state-owned Tier-IV national data centre at Kaliakoir (BDCCL), with little dedicated AI/GPU capacity

universities.name: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET)
universities.description: The country's leading engineering university; its CSE department hosts a prominent NLP group producing Bangla and multilingual language-model and dataset research.

universities.name: University of Dhaka
universities.description: Bangladesh's oldest university, active in Bangla NLP and AI-adjacent computer-science research.

universities.name: BRAC University
universities.description: Private Dhaka university with dedicated data-science and machine-learning tracks and Bengali NLP research collaborations; also home to the policy-research institute BIGD.

universities.name: American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB)
universities.description: Private university hosting an AI & Machine Learning research group within its computer-science department and engaged in AI-governance capacity work.

thinkTanks.name: Tech Global Institute
thinkTanks.description: Diaspora-founded nonprofit policy lab focused on technology governance in the Global South, which has published research on reforming AI laws and regulation in Bangladesh and engaged in UN-level AI-governance discussions.

thinkTanks.name: BRAC Institute of Governance and Development (BIGD)
thinkTanks.description: BRAC University-based social-science and governance research institute engaged in digital-governance and AI-policy analysis, and convenor of a policy-research consortium.

thinkTanks.name: Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD)
thinkTanks.description: Long-established independent Dhaka think tank (founded 1993) contributing economic and digital-economy policy analysis relevant to Bangladesh's AI and outsourcing agenda.

governmentInstitutions.name: Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology
governmentInstitutions.description: Lead ministry for Bangladesh's digital, telecom and AI policy; under the BNP government its minister (Fakir Mahbub Anam Swapan, from February 2026) oversees finalisation of the national AI policy.

governmentInstitutions.name: ICT Division
governmentInstitutions.description: The Information and Communication Technology Division within the ministry; principal drafter of the National AI Policy and the earlier AI strategy, and parent of a2i and the Bangladesh Computer Council.

governmentInstitutions.name: a2i (Aspire to Innovate)
governmentInstitutions.description: Flagship digital-government and public-service-innovation programme of the ICT Division, historically UNDP-supported; reportedly being restructured into a more autonomous statutory 'Agency to Innovate' after the 2024 change of government.

governmentInstitutions.name: Bangladesh Data Center Company Limited (BDCCL)
governmentInstitutions.description: State-owned company operating the Tier-IV national data centre at Kaliakoir Hi-Tech Park, providing G-Cloud, storage and colocation for government and enterprise.

governmentInstitutions.name: Bangladesh Computer Council (BCC)
governmentInstitutions.description: Statutory ICT-development body under the ICT Division supporting national digital infrastructure, hi-tech parks and capacity-building.

governmentInstitutions.name: National Data Governance and Innovation Agency (NDGIA)
governmentInstitutions.description: Coordinating AI/data-governance body proposed by the draft National AI Policy 2026-2030; as of mid-2026 it is not yet established or operational.

notableGaps.note: No frontier or near-frontier foundation-model developer is based in Bangladesh; domestic effort is limited to a handful of firms (e.g. Hishab, Intelsense AI) and academic groups building Bengali-language models, and analysts note only a very small number of companies produce Bangla LLMs despite 170m-plus speakers.

The National Data Governance and Innovation Agency proposed by the draft AI policy does not yet exist operationally, and there is no dedicated AI safety institute; oversight would rest on bodies that are not yet stood up.

As of mid-2026 the National AI Policy 2026-2030 remains a draft carried across the change of government, so no binding AI statute or policy is formally in force — governance leans on the new data-protection and cyber-security laws instead.
AI compute is nascent and concentrated in a single state-owned national data centre, with dedicated AI/GPU capacity thin and advanced chips fully import-reliant.

debates.topic: Whether an ambitious draft AI policy can survive Bangladesh's institutional-capacity and political-transition gap
debates.summary: The National AI Policy 2026-2030 is comparatively sophisticated on paper — risk tiers, prohibited uses, algorithmic impact assessments — but it was drafted under an interim government, remains unadopted, and depends on institutions (notably the NDGIA) that do not yet exist.
debates.expanded: Analysts point to an 'implementation gap': Bangladesh's earlier 2019-2020 AI strategy included detailed roadmaps that largely did not materialise, and the new policy's coordinating agency lacks a legal mandate or operational existence. The August 2024 change of government also disrupted the digital-government machinery — the ICT Division suspended a number of a2i officials and consultants, and a2i itself is being reorganised into a more autonomous statutory agency, raising questions about continuity of expertise. With the elected BNP government now saying it will finalise its own 'human-centric' AI policy, the open question is whether political ownership across the transition strengthens or dilutes the draft's more binding provisions.

debates.topic: Data-protection and cyber laws that critics argue protect the state more than citizens
debates.summary: Bangladesh has, in quick succession, enacted its first data-protection law and replaced the controversial 2023 Cyber Security Act — but civil-society and industry groups warn that broad state exemptions and surveillance powers persist.
debates.expanded: The Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2025 (later the 2026 Act) was praised for finally codifying data rights, yet critics — including domestic commentators and international bodies — highlight expansive carve-outs for the state and law enforcement, executive control over the oversight authority, and data-localisation rules tightened by a February 2026 amendment that could raise compliance costs and cross-border-data friction. The Cyber Security Ordinance 2025 struck out several speech-criminalising provisions of the 2023 Act, but rights groups argue residual powers still bear on AI-generated content, platform governance and freedom of expression. Together the reforms mark real progress while leaving contested questions about state power unresolved.

debates.topic: A vast freelancer and BPO workforce exposed to AI automation, with thin domestic Bengali-model capacity
debates.summary: Bangladesh's economic AI story rests on one of the world's largest online-freelancer and BPO workforces, whose IT-services exports are approaching US$1bn — but much of that work is exactly the kind AI could automate, while the country builds few Bengali-language models of its own.
debates.expanded: The freelancer/BPO base is a genuine national asset and a growing export earner, and an 'AI push' is being credited with lifting outsourcing revenues. Yet the same data-entry, transcription, moderation and back-office tasks are increasingly automatable, creating a strategic tension between riding AI demand and being displaced by it. Compounding this, domestic capacity to build sovereign Bengali AI is limited: only a small number of firms train Bangla-specific large language models despite the language's enormous speaker base, and the draft policy's call to prioritise domestically hosted Bangla models sits against thin compute and funding.

debates.topic: Reliance on a single national data centre and new data-localisation rules for 'sovereign' AI
debates.summary: Bangladesh's public-sector cloud and 'sovereign AI' ambitions lean heavily on one state-owned Tier-IV national data centre, even as new data-localisation rules push more data to be kept in-country.
debates.expanded: The BDCCL national data centre at Kaliakoir Hi-Tech Park — promoted domestically as among the world's larger Tier-IV facilities — anchors government G-Cloud services and is central to narratives about hosting Bangla-specific AI at home. But concentrating national data and compute in a single facility raises resilience and capacity questions, and the country still lacks meaningful dedicated AI/GPU infrastructure. The 2026 data-localisation amendments requiring in-country copies of restricted and critical-infrastructure data add both a sovereignty rationale and practical strain on this limited footprint, at a time when hyperscale cloud is served from outside Bangladesh.
